title: OOM sleuthing and allocator behavior walkthrough
content:
Summary:
- Running inference on some long-tail customer workloads we hit intermittent OOMs despite total GPU allocation being under cluster capacity. This is a working log of the investigation into allocator behavior, small-allocation churn, and workspace sizing that led to fragmentation and eventual cudaMalloc failures.

Symptoms observed:
- Sudden cudaMalloc failures in the middle of a stable request stream (not correlated with peak QPS).
- GPU memory reported by nvidia-smi showed free memory but CUDA calls returned OOM (cudaErrorMemoryAllocation).
- Crashes reproducible on  A100 in labs and in one dedicated cluster.
- OOMs more frequent when model context windows vary (lots of short requests interleaved with occasional long sequences).

Quick hypothesis:
- Fragmentation in the GPU allocator / caching layer (PyTorch caching allocator or runtime driver) leading to many small free blocks that cannot satisfy a larger contiguous cudaMalloc.
- Excessive transient allocations from token-level workspace or attention KV allocations during long requests create fragmentation patterns.
- cudaMalloc/cudaFree pattern (many small mallocs) + caching arenas can lead to internal splitting/unsuitable binning.

Repro steps we used:
1) Reproduce script: run many parallel requests that alternate between seq_len 32 and seq_len 4, inject occasional seq_len 2048.
2) Repro harness flags: set REQUESTS=2000 PAR=8; run until OOM seen or complete 2000 requests.
3) Capture logs: enable NVTX ranges around model forward/backward (inference) and write allocator stats to stdout every 50 requests.

Commands and traces (snippets):
- nvidia-smi --query-gpu=memory.total,memory.used --format=csv -lms 1000 -> showed 12GB used / 40GB total at time of OOM.
- nsight compute / nsight systems: recorded many small device allocations in timeline, followed by large cudaMalloc failing.
- ptx allocator sampling: arena sizes reported (via torch.cuda.memory_summary()) showed many small cached blocks but not a single contiguous free region large enough.

Example log excerpt:
[2024-09-18 14:23:12] request 1324 seq=2048 started
[2024-09-18 14:23:12] allocator: arena 3: free_chunks=1024 total_free=6.4GB
[2024-09-18 14:23:12] cudaMalloc(1.5G) -> ERROR cudaErrorMemoryAllocation
[2024-09-18 14:23:12] Post-mortem: total_free=6.4GB but max_contiguous_free_chunk=420MB

What we profiled and tools used:
- torch.cuda.memory_summary() snapshots at key points.
- nvprof / nsight to look at device-side allocation timeline.
- custom allocator introspection in the runtime (exposed small debug counters for arena fragmentation).
- Heap profiling via CUDA driver API (cuMemGetInfo) + sampling of free block sizes (where possible).

Key observations:
- The caching allocator (PyTorch-style) keeps many small cached blocks in arenas. The sum of free memory can be large yet there is no single contiguous block for a large allocation.
- Frequent allocations of medium-sized tensors (hundreds of KB to a few MB) during attention workspace and KV cache updates cause splitting of free blocks across multiple arenas.
- Interleaving short and long sequences increases churn: short requests free blocks that are too small to be coalesced into larger ones before the next long request arrives.
- Using cudaMallocAsync (where available) reduced host-visible fragmentation but did not eliminate failures in our test environment because the backend pool still suffered bin-exhaustion for the requested size bin.

Experiments run and outcomes:
1) Disable caching allocator (use torch.cuda.set_per_process_memory_fraction / environment toggles)
   - Outcome: OOM frequency decreased in one run (less fragmentation) but overall throughput dropped ~15% due to more remote allocations and driver calls. Not a long-term solution.
2) Pre-allocated workspace pool per-stream (reserve big contiguous chunk and sub-allocate manually)
   - Outcome: eliminated the large cudaMalloc at runtime; stable under stress tests. Tradeoff: higher baseline reserved memory and complexity in allocator code path.
3) Tune arena size / PYTORCH_CUDA_ALLOC_CONF (max_split_size_mb)
   - Outcome: increasing max_split_size_mb reduced number of splits, lowered fragmentation in a few runs. Needs careful tuning per model and typical sequence length distribution.
4) Switch to cudaMallocAsync + cuMemPool (CUDA 11.2+)
   - Outcome: improved latency for many small alloc/free patterns and improved reuse. Still saw bin-mismatch failures when one-off very large allocations were requested and large contiguous region not present in pool.

Mitigations attempted (short term):
- Add guard rails: if request seq_len > threshold (e.g., > 1024) check for max contiguous free using a cheap heuristic before scheduling. If fail, route to fallback node or delay until defrag event.
- Pre-warm large allocations during low-traffic windows (create a large dummy tensor to exercise pool allocation and force coalescing behavior where supported).
- Introduce best-effort workspace reuse: keep a sticky large workspace per worker thread/stream that services large requests.
- Metrics: emit per-request max_contiguous_free_estimate and track P95 to detect degradation early.

Longer-term ideas:
- Implement an internal pooled allocator tuned for our workload: combination of large monotonic arenas for KV caches and small-slab allocators for transient tensors.
- Expose a config-driven workspace sizing policy that picks workspace sizes based on recent request distribution (adaptive).
- Automatic defragmentation heuristics: trigger pool rebuilds during low traffic, or proactively consolidate pools when fragmentation crosses threshold.
- Consider sharding long requests to multiple GPUs (model parallel short of full MP) when contiguous memory unavailable.

Open questions / TODOs:
- Can we reliably measure max contiguous free region from user-space without heavy driver calls? Need a short spike test to probe allocation availability (fast and reversible).
- Should Dedicated nodes expose a "fragmentation budget" metric per host for customers (so we can route heavy contiguous requests away)?
- Evaluate behavior under different CUDA versions (11.4 vs 12.x) and drivers; some fragmentation/async malloc semantics changed across versions.
- Follow up: run extended soak on Dedicated cluster with prealloc workspace enabled (ticket ENG-1189).

Quick action items:
- [Priya] add per-request max_contiguous_free_estimate metric (short-term probe) - due 2024-10-04
- [Ethan] run 72h soak with preallocated workspace on ded-01 cluster - due 2024-10-01
- [Maya] validate cudaMallocAsync behavior across CUDA 11.7 and 12.1 images - due 2024-09-25 (initial notes attached)

Notes on related tickets and docs:
- ENG-1123: initial customer incident that surfaced this failure pattern.
- GH PR 482: small runtime change adding NVTX ranges and allocator counters.
- confluence:serving-runtime-memory-wp: extended writeup (draft) with diagrams of arena fragmentation.

Closing thoughts:
- Fragmentation is subtle; sum(free) != usable for large contiguous allocations. For production inference we need a combination of telemetry (detect fragmentation early), conservative workspace sizing for worst-case requests, and smarter pooling strategies.
- Immediate pragmatic fix: sticky per-worker large workspace to eliminate the one-off large cudaMalloc on the hot path; follow with pool rework in medium-term roadmap.

Appendix: small checklist for reproducing locally:
- CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=0 python tools/oom_repro.py --par 8 --requests 2000 --mix "32:6,4:1,2048:1"
- capture torch.cuda.memory_summary() snapshots to /tmp/mem_snapshots
- run nsight systems for 30s windows around suspected failing requests

End of notes.
